video.title: I Thought I Understood Credit Cards Until I Talked to This Guy

summary: Host Chris Koerner interviews Brandon Elliot about using credit cards, bank relationships, and other bank products to obtain business funding, often at promotional interest rates. Elliot describes funding real estate, cleaning up credit profiles, and selling authorized-user access on credit cards. He also shares examples involving business auto loans, property investment, and construction. The main takeaway is that credit access can support business and property investments, but the process involves fees, careful timing, and substantial debt and compliance risks.

speakers.name: Brandon Elliot
speakers.description: Credit and business-funding educator; names Credit Council Elite and Brandon Elliot Investments.

ideas.name: Credit-card and bank funding advisory
ideas.one_liner: Teach or guide business owners and investors through building credit profiles and applying for bank funding, including promotional-rate credit cards.
ideas.business_model: Education, coaching, and member support; exact revenue model and fees are not stated.
ideas.customer: Business owners and real-estate investors seeking working capital or funding for vehicles and property.
ideas.problem: They need capital and may not know how to qualify for bank products or use promotional-rate credit responsibly.
ideas.offer: Guidance on credit profiles, bank relationships, application sequencing, funding products, and ways to access credit-card limits as cash.

pricing.model: Not stated; the guest mentions members and a live boot camp.
pricing.notes: The boot-camp ticket price and any membership or consulting fees are not stated.

acquisition_channels.details: The guest names Instagram pages Brandon Elliot Investments and Credit Council Elite. The transcript does not explain a specific content or conversion process.
The guest says the business runs a live boot camp once a month and gives capitalbootcamp.live as the event site.

quote.text: We do a live boot camp once a month. And so our next one coming up is actually it's October 5th through 9th.
quote.speaker: Brandon Elliot

acquisition_channels.details: Members are mentioned, but the channel used to recruit them is not stated.

quote.text: our goal is to show members how to actually get up to 500,000
quote.speaker: Brandon Elliot

ideas.delivery: The guest describes teaching members about credit and funding, with a monthly virtual live boot camp. The detailed support format, staffing, and division of work are not stated.
unit_economics_claims: The guest claims the process can obtain up to $500,000 in credit, sometimes at 0% promotional interest.
The guest says promotional periods commonly last 18 months on average, with a stated range of 6 to 24 months.
The guest says obtaining that level of funding may involve 10 to 50 or more applications.

acquisition.how: A virtual boot camp and social channels can attract inbound interest with routine software support. The transcript gives no evidence that lead generation or closing is unattended; relationship-based sales would still need human work.

onboarding.how: Collecting and reviewing a customer's credit profile, banking history, and goals could use forms and document tools, but the guest describes individualized financial circumstances and sequencing.

delivery.how: The main value is financial guidance and application sequencing, which require human judgment and careful review of the customer's circumstances and lender terms.

billing.how: Payment automation is technically feasible, but the transcript does not state how customers pay or whether the business has recurring billing.

support.how: Questions about credit profiles, bank rules, and application decisions are individualized and likely require human support.

uk_applicability.notes: The general idea of advising on business finance transfers, but the examples rely heavily on US banks, US credit reporting, and US card products. A UK version would need to account for UK lending, financial-promotion, and consumer-credit rules.

risks: Credit-card funding is debt, and promotional rates and fees depend on lender terms; the guest warns that ordinary cash advances can carry very high rates.
A missed payment, a new transaction on a card with a transferred balance, or failure to repay before a promotional period ends can create significant interest costs.
Application sequencing and credit utilization can affect access to future credit and personal credit scores.
UK financial advice, credit broking, and financial promotions may require specific permissions or compliance steps.
The guest promotes a boot camp and credit-related businesses, which creates a commercial incentive to present the strategy favorably.

ideas.name: Credit repair and credit-profile improvement service
ideas.one_liner: Help consumers review credit reports, challenge inaccurate entries, and improve their profiles before applying for credit.
ideas.business_model: Potential service or coaching offer; the guest says he is not a fan of the credit-repair industry and does not clearly claim to operate a standalone credit-repair business.
ideas.customer: People with late payments, collections, charge-offs, inquiries, or other credit-report issues who want to qualify for funding.
ideas.problem: Errors or negative marks can reduce credit scores and make lenders less willing to extend credit.
ideas.offer: Review reports, identify inaccurate information, prepare disputes, contact bureaus, and keep records of correspondence.

pricing.notes: No credit-repair service price is given.

ideas.delivery: The guest describes customers obtaining reports, identifying inaccurate entries, uploading or mailing disputes, and following up with bureaus. He also says AI can help draft letters. The transcript does not establish who performs this work as a paid service.

acquisition.how: Inbound search or educational content could attract customers, but the transcript does not state an acquisition method.

onboarding.how: Clients could submit reports and documents digitally, but personal review and identity verification would still be needed.

delivery.how: AI may help draft letters, but dispute grounds, documents, deadlines, and follow-up need human review. The guest says outcomes and timelines cannot be promised.

billing.how: Payments could be processed online, but no billing system or service terms are stated.

support.how: Dispute outcomes and bureau responses are case-specific and require human explanation and follow-up.

uk_applicability.notes: Reviewing and correcting credit-file inaccuracies is relevant in the UK, but the transcript's bureaus, dispute process, and legal references are US-specific and would need replacement with UK procedures.

risks: The guest says no one can legally promise a credit-repair timeline; avoid guarantees about score increases or removals.
The guest says some negative information may be accurate, and a dispute process does not ensure removal.
Handling credit reports and identity documents creates privacy and data-security obligations.
The guest discourages paying a collection solely to remove a negative mark; customers should verify the debt and understand local consequences before acting.
Credit repair is a crowded industry that the guest says often overpromises.

quotes.text: So, number one, you would typically want to get your credit report first, and you want to identify what's legitimate on there and what's not.
quotes.speaker: Brandon Elliot

ideas.name: Selling authorized-user credit-card access
ideas.one_liner: Earn money by adding paying customers as authorized users on an established credit card, allowing the account history to appear on their credit profiles.
ideas.business_model: Sell or lease authorized-user access through a tradeline intermediary or marketplace.
ideas.customer: People seeking to improve their credit profile before applying for funding.
ideas.problem: Customers may have a short credit history or too few accounts to meet the profile they want.
ideas.offer: Add a buyer as an authorized user for a limited period on a card with an established history, low balance, and good payment record.

pricing.model: Per authorized-user slot or time-limited lease.
pricing.notes: The guest says intermediaries may resell the access for much more. He does not name a marketplace.

acquisition_channels.details: The guest says there is an online tradeline industry and says he used to sell his own authorized-user spots there. No specific marketplace is named.

quote.text: I used to sell mine on there and I would make $125, you know, 200 bucks and then one time.
quote.speaker: Brandon Elliot

ideas.delivery: The seller gives an intermediary or buyer the required identifying information; the cardholder adds the buyer to the account, may activate a card, and the account history is reported to credit bureaus. The guest says the buyer does not receive account login or spending access.
unit_economics_claims: The guest says he earned $125 or $200 for some sales, while an intermediary once resold access for $2,000.
The guest says a card may have five to ten authorized-user slots and that access is typically leased for about 60 days.

acquisition.how: A marketplace can handle discovery and some matching, but the seller still needs to qualify buyers and manage the cardholder relationship.

onboarding.how: The guest describes collecting full name, date of birth, Social Security number, address, and phone number; sensitive identity handling requires careful human oversight.

delivery.how: The account holder must arrange and manage authorized-user access. Account reporting and removal are controlled by the card issuer and bureau.

billing.how: A marketplace could automate payment collection, but no platform or payment workflow is named.

support.how: Disputes, reporting issues, and changes to the primary cardholder's account need human intervention.

uk_applicability.notes: The described process depends on US credit bureaus, Social Security numbers, and US authorized-user reporting practices. Any UK analogue would need separate validation and privacy, credit, and consumer-law review.

risks: The buyer shares sensitive identity details, while the seller retains control of the account.
A high balance, missed payment, or other adverse change on the primary account can harm the buyer's credit profile.
The guest's claim that the seller faces no risk should not be treated as a guarantee; card issuers can change how authorized-user accounts are handled.
The practice may not transfer to UK credit-reporting systems, and misleading promises about score improvement could create legal and reputational risk.

quotes.text: I used to sell mine on there and I would make $125, you know, 200 bucks and then one time. Yeah. And they would they would sell it for like 2,000.

ideas.name: Rental-property investment using credit funding
ideas.one_liner: Use credit funding to acquire or improve rental property, refinance after value is added, and repeat the process.
ideas.business_model: Property investment with rental income, refinancing, and potential appreciation; the guest says he uses the BRRRR strategy.
ideas.customer: Not stated as a customer-facing business; the investor is the operator, with tenants as the rental customers.
ideas.problem: Investors need capital for property acquisition and renovation and want to recycle capital into further investments.
ideas.offer: Buy, renovate, rent, refinance, and repeat; the guest says he has used credit cards to fund real-estate projects.

pricing.model: Rental income and property refinancing; rents and financing terms are not stated.
pricing.notes: No rental prices, property purchase prices for his own projects, or operating costs are stated.

acquisition_channels.details: Property acquisition method is not stated. The guest describes the investment and financing approach rather than how he sources properties or tenants.

quote.text: What we do is we use a lot of it for real estate. I've always done the burr strategy. Buy, renovate, rent, refinance, repeat.
quote.speaker: Brandon Elliot

ideas.delivery: The operator acquires and renovates property, rents it, then seeks to refinance and recycle capital. Renovation and property management involve physical-world work.
unit_economics_claims: The guest says he has used credit cards to buy real estate and has used the BRRRR strategy; project-level returns are not stated.

acquisition.how: Listings and property data can be monitored by software, but underwriting and purchase decisions need human review.

onboarding.how: Property financing, inspections, and purchase paperwork require human coordination.

delivery.how: Renovation, maintenance, and property operations require people on site.

billing.how: Rent and loan payments can be scheduled digitally, though no system is stated.

support.how: Tenant issues and property repairs require human judgment and often physical work.

uk_applicability.notes: The buy-renovate-rent-refinance concept applies in the UK, but lending, property, tax, planning, and landlord rules differ. The guest's US credit products and examples do not transfer directly.

risks: Using revolving debt for property investment exposes the operator to interest-rate, refinancing, valuation, vacancy, and renovation risks.
The guest's strategy depends on successfully refinancing; a lender or valuation change could prevent capital from being recycled.
UK landlords and property investors must account for local property, tax, and planning requirements.

quotes.text: What we do is we use a lot of it for real estate. I've always done the burr strategy. Buy, renovate, rent, refinance, repeat.

ideas.name: Ground-up residential construction and refinance
ideas.one_liner: Fund residential construction, build property, and refinance after completion to recover capital.

ideas.customer: Not stated; the guest describes construction and refinancing as an investment activity.
ideas.problem: The investor needs capital to build property and wants to recover the funds after construction.
ideas.offer: The guest says he uses credit cards for ground-up construction in San Diego and refinances after the build.

pricing.notes: The guest gives claimed construction cost and post-build value per square foot, but not project size or final realized sale price.

ideas.delivery: The operator funds and manages ground-up construction, completes the build, and applies for cash-out refinancing. Construction is physical work and depends on contractors and local approvals.

acquisition.how: Land and project opportunities can be found online, but acquisition and feasibility decisions require human review.

onboarding.how: Financing, planning, contractor, and site processes need human coordination.

delivery.how: Construction is physical-world work and cannot be delivered by software alone.

billing.how: Invoices and financing payments can use software, but construction spending and lender draw processes require oversight.

support.how: Contractor, permitting, and lender issues require human intervention.

uk_applicability.notes: Ground-up development is possible in the UK, but the guest's San Diego costs and valuations are location-specific. UK planning, building regulations, labour costs, finance, and property values would need new analysis.

risks: The guest's construction cost and value estimates are location-specific claims and do not establish realized profit.
Construction, planning, financing, contractor, and valuation risks can leave an investor with more debt than expected.
The transcript does not state project size, time to completion, or whether the stated value is realized in a sale.

tactics.name: Build bank relationships before applying
steps: Keep bank accounts open and use them actively rather than letting balances sit without transactions.
The guest says banks may look at transaction volume, average balance, and whether more money comes in than goes out.
Build relationships with large banks first, then regional banks, then local credit unions.
Use the guest's stated Chase rules as examples of lender-specific application limits, and check current terms before applying.

quote.text: So, how we break it down is three levels. Big banks first, regional banks second, small local credit unions last.
quote.speaker: Brandon Elliot

tactics.name: Prepare an auto purchase before visiting the dealership
steps: The guest suggests seeking business auto-loan pre-approval first.
Visit near the last day of the month, about two to three hours before closing, when sales staff may be focused on quota.
The guest suggests asking for a salesperson who is near the bottom of the dealership's leaderboard.
Treat this as a negotiation tactic, not a guarantee of a lower price.

quote.text: And then also looking each dealership has like a uh leadership board. And so you want to look for that
quote.speaker: Brandon Elliot

tactics.name: Use promotional balance transfers carefully
steps: Ask the issuer whether a credit limit can be transferred to a bank account at a promotional rate.
Confirm the rate, fee, promotional end date, minimum payments, and whether new transactions are allowed.
Do not assume a standard cash advance has the same rate as a promotional transfer.
Avoid using a card for a new transaction when the guest says that could trigger interest on the balance.

quote.text: you want to make sure it's at a promotional rate. If you don't do that, then it's going to end up being the mafia rates of 20, 30, 40%.
quote.speaker: Brandon Elliot

tactics.name: Review and build a credit profile in sequence
steps: Review the credit report and separate accurate information from entries that may be wrong.
Address late payments, collections, charge-offs, or other issues before relying on account-building tactics.
The guest recommends monitoring payment timing, utilization, account age, and account mix.
Treat the guest's score targets and timelines as claims, not guaranteed outcomes.

quote.text: You have to do fix otherwise it's lipstick on a pig, right? Because people do that out there, too.
quote.speaker: Brandon Elliot

tactics.name: Document credit-report disputes
steps: Obtain reports from the relevant bureaus and identify entries that appear inaccurate.
Submit a dispute with supporting documents through the bureau's stated process.
Keep copies, dates, certified-mail numbers, and tracking information.
Do not promise a specific removal or improvement timeline.

quote.text: if they keep giving you stall tactics, you're going to want to have like clear certified mail numbers and and tracking and everything dialed in
quote.speaker: Brandon Elliot

tactics.name: Screen authorized-user accounts and limit exposure
steps: The guest says an account should have a long history, low balance, and no late payments.
Explain that a buyer does not receive spending access but shares sensitive identity details to be added.
Agree on the duration and removal process in advance.
Monitor changes in the primary cardholder's account because a balance spike or late payment can affect the added user's profile.

quote.text: it's got to be good. Like, it's got to be no late payments collection. like it's got to be in good status, long history, ideally large limit, and low balance.
quote.speaker: Brandon Elliot

tactics.name: Use a property-investment capital cycle
steps: The guest describes buying, renovating, renting, refinancing, and repeating.
Model the project around renovation cost, rental income, refinance terms, valuation, and debt repayment.
The guest says he uses credit funding for real estate, but provides no project-level return calculation.

quote.text: I've always done the burr strategy. Buy, renovate, rent, refinance, repeat.

tactics.name: Treat aged-entity offers skeptically
steps: Do not treat an aged entity as sufficient for funding approval.
The guest says lenders consider multiple underwriting factors and that entity history is only one part.
Avoid sellers promising very large funding outcomes for a high upfront payment.
